In 1989, the year the Berlin Wall fell, West Germany's GDP per capita was about $17,700.

East Germany's was about $5,100 — and East Germany was the star pupil of the socialist bloc.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ The red bloc, in nominal dollars: USSR ~$2,711. Poland ~$2,229. Hungary ~$3,115. Czechoslovakia ~$3,764. Romania ~$2,477. Yugoslavia ~$4,197. Albania ~$904, the poorest figure on the map by a distance.

2/ The blue side: Switzerland above $30,000, Sweden ~$25,300, Finland ~$24,300, Norway ~$24,000, Denmark ~$21,900. France ~$17,700, Britain ~$16,300, Italy ~$16,200. A gap of roughly five to ten times.

3/ But nominal dollar figures flatter the West badly. Socialist currencies weren't convertible and their exchange rates were set by decree, not markets. Converting a rouble or a zloty at the official rate produces a number that means very little.

4/ Purchasing-power estimates narrow the gap a lot — Czechoslovakia and Hungary land nearer half of Western European levels rather than a fifth. Housing, transport and bread were heavily subsidised; queues and shortages don't show up in either number.

5/ The honest comparisons are the ones the map sets up by accident. Austria ~$17,300 against Czechoslovakia ~$3,764: neighbours, similar industrial bases in 1938. West Germany against East Germany: the same country, split for 40 years.

6/ And the map cuts the other way too. Turkey, capitalist, sits at ~$2,714 — essentially level with the USSR. Portugal ~$6,129 and Greece ~$7,864 were poorer than the richer socialist states looked on some measures. The line wasn't only ideological.

7/ Within two years of this snapshot, most of the red had gone — and the decade that followed was brutal for much of it. Output in several post-Soviet states didn't return to 1989 levels until the mid-2000s.

Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
